paragraphs: Ulla.

Hyman argues: Without any doubt, the plain “Ulla” always mentioned in the Babylonian Talmud is Ulla bar Yishmael, who is always mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud; only in one place in the Babylonian Talmud has his name together with his father’s name remained for us, as in Sanhedrin 92a. Proof of this we find in Sukkah 4:5: “Ulla bar Yishmael in the name of Rabbi Elazar: festival peace offerings slaughtered on the eve of the festival — one does not fulfill one’s obligation with them”; and in Pesachim 70a this saying is in the name of “Ulla said that Rabbi Elazar said.”

Likewise Jerusalem Talmud Gittin, chapter 5, end of halakhah 6, Ulla bar Yishmael on this law: “even if it did not become known to the public, it does not atone,” etc.; and in Gittin 55a it appears in the name of plain Ulla. Hyman identifies his father as Rabbi Yishmael, who was a great sage, as explained in his entry.

In Shabbat 13a it is related of him that when he came from the house of study he would kiss his sisters on their bosom, and some say on their hands. In Hyman’s account, he further merited to receive from the mouths of the sages of the first generation of Amoraim, as we find “Ulla said that Rabbi Oshaya said,” as in Chullin 76a. He also called him “Rabbi Hoshayah, the father of the Mishnah, explained it so,” as in Yevamot 3:3. “Ulla said that Rabbi Chanina said,” as in Menachot 30b. “Ulla said that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said,” as in Chullin 122a.
In the name of Rabbi Yitzchak, as in Nedarim 4:2 (and there “Ulla bar Yishmael”).
Likewise he said, “I was standing before Ben Pazi,” in Chullin 47a.

Likewise Ulla said, “Ben Zakkai said,” as in Chullin 52a. Ulla in the name of Bar Padda, as in Kiddushin 54b. “Ulla said that Rav said,” as in Shabbat 143b. Ulla in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, as in Taanit 22b.

Hyman identifies Rabbi Yochanan as his principal teacher, citing Chagigah 19a: “Ulla said: I asked Rabbi Yochanan — and he said to me,” etc.; and as in Nedarim 22a: “When Ulla came before Rabbi Yochanan — he said to him,” etc.

In Mevo ha-Yerushalmi, page 150, he says that we do not find that Ulla spoke with Rabbi Yochanan face to face, and therefore there is room for doubt whether he was his student; Hyman calls this an oversight.

Likewise we find “Ulla said that Rabbi Yochanan said,” as in Berakhot 38b, 51b and 58b; Shabbat 3a; Eruvin 66b; Yevamot 77a; Gittin 39a and 79a; Kiddushin 38b and 60a; Sanhedrin 47a; Avodah Zarah 55a; Zevachim 14b; Chullin 46b, 76b and 125a; and Me’ilah 2a.
Likewise he disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan, as in Chullin 122a.
Likewise he received much from Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, as we find “Ulla said that Resh Lakish said,” as in Pesachim 56b, Chagigah 8b, Gittin 50b, Bava Metzia 9b and 101a, and Zevachim 32b.
Likewise “Ulla said that Rabbi Elazar said,” as in Eruvin 21b, Pesachim 70b, Ketubot 74a, Gittin 20a, Bava Kamma 11a and 11b several times, Sanhedrin 47a and Zevachim 14b.

Likewise Ulla said, “Rabbi Elazar raised an objection,” as in Shabbat 44b; and in the Jerusalem Talmud, Ulla bar Yishmael in the name of Rabbi Elazar, as in Maaserot, beginning of chapter 3, and 5:2, Kilayim 9:2, Shabbat 1:3, Chagigah 1:4 and Sukkah 4:5.

Hyman writes that he was appointed by Rabbi Yochanan’s academy in the Land of Israel and by Rav Yehudah’s academy in Babylonia to bring the Torah of each academy to the other, and in the Jerusalem Talmud he was called “Ulla the Descender” (Ulla Nachuta), as in Kilayim, chapter 9, end of halakhah 3. This is what they said in Berakhot 9b: Rabbi Elazar said to Ulla, “When you go there (to Babylonia), ask after the welfare of Rav Beruna my brother.”
Likewise we find in Berakhot 26b, Shabbat 108b, Rosh Hashanah 20a and 22b, and Sanhedrin 63a: “When Ulla came.”

He was so great in the eyes of the sages of Babylonia that Rav Chisda said of him, Berakhot 38a, “our Rabbis who come down from the Land of Israel — and who is that? Ulla.” Hyman places this in Rabbi Yochanan’s lifetime, as is related in Nedarim 22a: when Ulla was going up to the Land of Israel, two men of Mechoza [בני מחוזא] joined him. One rose and slaughtered his fellow, and said to Ulla, “Did I do well?” He said to him, “Yes, and expose the place of slaughter for him.” When he came before Rabbi Yochanan, Ulla said, “Perhaps, God forbid, I strengthened the hands of transgressors?” He (Rabbi Yochanan) said to him, “You saved your life.”

Hyman argues that one cannot mistakenly say that he was a native of Babylonia and that this was the first time he went up to the Land of Israel, for it is stated explicitly in Taanit 9b: Ulla happened to come to Babylonia; he saw scattered clouds and said, “Clear away the vessels, for now the rain is coming.” In the end it did not come. He said, “Just as the Babylonians lie, so their rains lie.”

Likewise Pesachim 88b: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita; they brought before him a basket of dates. He said to them, “How many like these for a zuz?” They said to him, “Three for a zuz.” He said, “A basketful of honey for a zuz, and the Babylonians do not engage in Torah!” At night they troubled him; he said, “A basketful of deadly poison for a zuz in Babylonia, and the Babylonians engage in Torah!”
Likewise Rosh Hashanah 20a: Ulla said, “Do our Babylonian colleagues know what favor we do for them?”

In Bava Kamma 38a: Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah’s daughter died. The Rabbis said to Ulla, “Rise, let us go and comfort him.” He said to them, “What have I to do with the consolation of the Babylonians, which is blasphemy?” (meaning that he did not wish to go with them). He went by himself to him, etc. Hyman concludes: From all this we see clearly that he was not a native of Babylonia and did not know the nature of the land and its fruits.

Likewise they said in Jerusalem Talmud Demai, chapter 1: “Ulla bar Yishmael in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — Ulla went down there and said it in Rabbi Yochanan’s name.” In Hyman’s account, in his coming to Babylonia he did not settle in one place but went from academy to academy to transmit there the Torah of the Land of Israel, and especially he was with Rav Yehudah in Pumbedita, as in Kiddushin 71b: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita to the house of Rav Yehudah; he saw Rav Yitzchak, Rav Yehudah’s son, who was grown and not married, etc.
Likewise Shabbat 146a: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita — Rav Yehudah said to him, etc.
Likewise Pesachim 88a and Taanit 9a: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita, etc.
In Beitzah 22a: Ulla happened to come to Rav Yehudah’s house — they raised an objection to Ulla.
In Pesachim 104b: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita; Rav Yehudah sent his son Rav Yitzchak to see how Ulla performs havdalah, and sent with him a basket of fruit.
He was very dear to Rav Yehudah, as in Chullin 94a: when he happened to come to Rav Yehudah’s house, he opened for him barrels of wine, because Ulla was dear to Rav Yehudah.

Likewise Ulla greatly honored Rav Yehudah, as in Niddah 20b: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita; they brought blood before him and he would not examine it (out of respect for Rav Yehudah), although he was a great expert in bloods, as they said there, 20a: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita; he saw a certain Arab dressed in a black garment and said to them, “The black that we learned of is like this.” They tore off a little from it and paid four hundred zuz for it. Hyman concludes: From this we can see his greatness and wisdom in the eyes of the sages of the academy.
Likewise he debated with Rav Yehudah many times in halakhot, as in Kiddushin 38b, Avodah Zarah 53b, and Chullin 76a and 65b; and Rav Yehudah said in Ulla’s name, as in Avodah Zarah 40a.
In Gittin 19b we find Rav Yehudah taking pains to read and sign; Ulla said to him, “You do not need to.”

Likewise we find him with Rav Nachman, as in Berakhot 51a: Ulla happened to come to Rav Nachman’s house; he ate bread and recited the Grace after Meals, etc., and Yalta was angry with him and called him one of the “peddlers of words” (because he went from place to place). Rav Nachman called him “master,” as in Bava Metzia 9b and Chullin 76b; he raised a difficulty to Ulla, as in Shabbat 39b, Gittin 66b and Chullin 124a; he raised an objection to Ulla, as in Zevachim 16a; Rav Nachman and Ulla were sitting, as in Ketubot 53a and Avodah Zarah 63a; Rav Nachman called him “Ulla our colleague,” as in Berakhot 38b; and in Pesachim 80a Rav Nachman said to them, “Go and say to Ulla, who will listen,” etc. In Bava Kamma 12a, Ulla said that Rabbi Elazar said, “The halakhah is,” etc.; Rav Nachman said to him, “Did Rabbi Elazar say so even with regard to orphans?” — Rav Nachman said, “Ulla evaded me” (slipped away from me). Their dispute: Kiddushin 44b.

Likewise we find that he happened to come to Rav Menasheh’s house, as in Eruvin 104b; he happened to come to Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah’s house, as in Shabbat 109b, and went to comfort him, as in Bava Kamma 38b; and he called Ulla “master.”

Likewise we find: Ulla happened to come to the Exilarch’s house and saw Rabbah bar Rav Huna sitting in a tub of water, etc. — end of Shabbat. He happened to come to the house of Assi bar Hini, who asked him; Ulla said to him, “So said Rabbi Ilai,” as in Shabbat 146a.
He brought many customs and several laws from the Land of Israel, as in Rosh Hashanah 20a, where he said, “They intercalated Elul”; and there, 22a, he said, “They sanctified the month in the West.”

And as in Shabbat 85b and Bava Metzia 105b, “they asked in the West”; and as in Shabbat 108b, when Ulla came he said, “In the West they salt pile after pile [כישרי כישרי]”; and in Pesachim 93b, “from Modi’im to Jerusalem is fifteen mil.”
And as in Chagigah 25a: “The fellowship purifies in the Galilee.”

In Gittin 57a he said: “I myself saw that place, and it does not hold even sixty myriads of reeds.” He also issued rulings in Babylonia, as in Eruvin 6b, where he said, “These gateways of Mechoza — were it not that their doors are locked at night, one would be liable for them for carrying in the public domain”; and in Sukkah 20b, “these mats of the people of Mechoza — were it not for their upturned rim, one could use them for the sukkah covering.”

Hyman writes: He was so great that they called him “Ulla Rabbah” (Ulla the Great), as in Ketubot 65b: Ulla Rabbah expounded at the entrance of the Nasi’s house (that is, the Exilarch): “Although they said a man does not feed,” etc. And in Kiddushin 31a: Ulla Rabbah expounded at the entrance of the Nasi’s house — “When the Holy One, blessed be He, said ‘I am’ and ‘You shall have no,’ they said,” etc. His halakhot and sayings fill the whole Talmud, Babylonian and Jerusalem, and we shall bring only a few sayings on aggadic matters.

In Berakhot 8a he said: “From the day the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing but the four cubits of halakhah alone.” “Greater is one who benefits from his own labor than one who fears Heaven.” “A person should always dwell in the place of his teacher.”
He said the famous parable, “A coin in a jar cries ‘kish, kish,’” as in Bava Metzia 85b.

Hyman writes: Now although he did not merit to become head of an academy, he was so great and held so many halakhot from his teachers that all the great men of the generation received from him, such as Rabbi Abba, who raised an objection to Ulla, and he said to him, “This one of the Rabbis seems like people who have not learned the teaching,” as in Gittin 39a and Bava Metzia 11a. Rabbi Abba raised difficulties to him, as in Gittin 50b and 79a and Kiddushin 58a.

In Pesachim 53b it is related: Ulla was riding a donkey, and Rabbi Abba was walking on his right and Rabbah bar bar Chanah on his left. Rabbi Abba said to Ulla, “Is it true that you say in Rabbi Yochanan’s name,” etc. Abaye further merited in his youth to see him, as is related in Pesachim 104b: when Ulla came to Pumbedita, Rav Yehudah sent Rav Yitzchak his son to go to Ulla and hear how he performs havdalah, and Rav Yitzchak sent Abaye. And as in Sanhedrin 30b:

when Ulla said, “The halakhah follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah” — Abaye said to him, “‘The halakhah’ implies that they disagree, but did not … say,” etc. — he said to him, “You set one man against another.” Hyman concludes that Abaye was undoubtedly still young at the time.
Rabbi Avina (in the name of) Ulla bar Yishmael in the name of Rabbi Elazar, as in Maaserot 5:2 and Shabbat 1:3.

Rav Adda bar Ahavah in Ulla’s name, as in Bava Kamma 55a — Hyman finds this very hard to understand, as it is known that he was Rav’s distinguished student, and Dikdukei Soferim’s reading, Rav Acha bar Adda, is more correct.
Rav Oshaya raised an objection to Ulla, as in Gittin 16b.
In Zevachim 32b it reads Rav Hoshaya. Their dispute: Gittin 77b.
Rav Acha bar Adda in his name, as in Bava Metzia 117b.

And so, Hyman proposes, it should read in Bava Kamma 55a, according to the reading of Dikdukei Soferim. Rav Huna bar Chiyya in his name, as in Nedarim 56a. Rav Hamnuna sat before Ulla and was engaged in a teaching, as in Yevamot 17; he said in Ulla’s name, as in Shabbat 10b, Gittin 5a and Kiddushin 78b; he raised an objection to Ulla, as in Nedarim 29a and Chullin 34b.
Rabbi Zeira sat before Ulla, and Rabbah asked Rabbi Zeira to ask Ulla, as in Pesachim 36b.

We find in Avodah Zarah 40a: Ulla raised a contradiction for Rabbi Dostai of Biri — “strike out from here ‘okhran,’” Rabbi Zeira said to him, “Do not strike it out,” etc. And Maaser Sheni 2:3: Rabbi Ze’ira said, “I saw in a dream that Ulla bar Yishmael was given fat meat [קופרא שמינא] (in Hyman’s interpretation, meaning that he knows the reason for the matter)”; the next day he came and asked him, etc.
Rav Chaga raised an objection to Ulla. Ulla replied, “[Chani?] does not know what the Rabbis are saying, yet he raises an objection?” as in Avodah Zarah 68a; he said in Ulla’s name, as in Gittin 23a.
Rav Chiyya bar Abba in his name, as in Chagigah 25b.
Rav Chiyya bar Ami in his name, as in Berakhot 8a and Shabbat 17a; he sat with Ulla, as in Ketubot 53a and Avodah Zarah 63b.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Assi in his name, as in Gittin 22a.
Rav Yehudah bar Ami in his name, as in Moed Katan 5b.
Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba in his name, as in Shabbat 126a and Moed Katan 5b.
Rabbi Yonah (in the name of) Ulla bar Yishmael in the name of Rabbi Elazar, as in Kilayim 9:1 and Sukkah 4:5.

Rav Yosef — as in Pesachim 36b: Rabbah and Rav Yosef sat behind Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbi Zeira sat before Ulla; in Sanhedrin 30b, Rav Yosef said in Ulla’s name; and in Pesachim 53b Rav Yosef applied to him the verse [preceded in the supplied text by the isolated word דולה, “draws out”] “Counsel in a man’s heart is deep water” — this is Ulla.
Rav Kahana called Ulla “a great man,” as in Rosh Hashanah 22b; he said in his name, as in Ketubot 74b.
Rav Ulla bar Abba said that Ulla said, as in Ketubot 74a.

Rav Amram said, “This matter I heard from Ulla,” as in Gittin 26b. Rava we find many times with Ulla, but Hyman identifies that as the later Ulla, as explained in his entry. Rabbah — in Pesachim 36b Rabbah said to Rabbi Zeira, “Ask Ulla.” Rabbah said to Ulla, as in Shabbat 31b, Eruvin 104a, Pesachim 56b and Moed Katan 26a. Rabbah said to him, “For you it is difficult and for Rav Yehudah it is difficult,” as in Pesachim 93b. Rabbah bar bar Chanah — in Pesachim 53b: Ulla was riding a donkey, and Rabbi Abba was on his right and Rabbah bar bar Chanah on his left — then Ulla looked upon Rabbah bar bar Chanah with displeasure, etc. Ravin bar Chanana said that Ulla said, as in Menachot 30b. Hyman writes that nothing of his private affairs has remained for us; only this is known, that he died in Babylonia in the lifetime of Rabbi Elazar, as in Ketubot 111a, where they said: Ulla was accustomed to go up to the Land of Israel; he died outside the Land. They came and told Rabbi Elazar. He lamented, quoting the verse, “You, Ulla, shall die on an unclean land,” and they brought his coffin to the Land of Israel.

Likewise it is in Kilayim, chapter 9, end of halakhah 3: Ulla Nachuta was dying there and began to weep. They said to him, “Why do you weep? We will bring you up to the Land of Israel.” He said to them, “It is not the same to give up one’s life in one’s mother’s bosom as to give it up in the bosom of a stranger.”
We find Rav Acha son of Ulla, Shabbat 54b; Rava or Rabbah son of Ulla, Berakhot 12a and Yevamot 77.

The supplied citation points to the end of Jerusalem Talmud Gittin 5:6. The consulted edition names Ulla bar Yishmael and has a bracketed gap before “became known to the public.” Bavli Gittin 55a names Ulla without a patronymic and distinguishes the underlying rule from the practical exception for a case that did not become known. Hyman uses the parallel in his argument about Ulla’s identity.

The printed page (Hyman III, p. 971) reads Chagigah 19a where the supplied transcription has ים. The consulted Chagigah 19a contains both Ulla’s question to Rabbi Yochanan and the reply. The claim that Rabbi Yochanan was his principal teacher and the criticism of Mevo ha-Yerushalmi are Hyman’s judgments. Hyman’s locator for the latter work is page 150.

Hyman’s printed page 971 names two men of Mechoza and cites Berakhot 38a. The consulted Nedarim 22a names two men of Bei Chozai, and Rav Chisda’s expression appears in the consulted Berakhot 38b. Both the printed geography and the edition difference matter to Hyman’s argument.
Printed page 973 has ובל״ס (“and undoubtedly”), where the supplied transcription has וכל״ס. Sanhedrin 30b has the exchange between Ulla and Abaye. Abaye’s youth at this point is Hyman’s inference.

The printed text cites Pesachim 36b in these notices. The conversation is at Pesachim 37b in the consulted edition, where Rabbah directs Rabbi Zeira to ask Ulla. Printed page 974 has the abbreviation for Rabbi Zeira twice where the supplied transcription has Rav Nachman. The print also has the isolated דולה before the quotation. In the consulted Pesachim 53b–54a the first part of the verse is applied to Ulla and its continuation to Rabbah bar bar Chanah.

On printed page 973 the introduction names Rav Chaga. The start of Ulla’s reply appears as חני, and the person criticized fails to understand what the Rabbis are saying. The supplied text instead has הני and ורבנן. The consulted Avodah Zarah 68a names Chaga in the reply as well.

Printed page 974 ends the notice after the reference to Yevamot 77. A separate heading begins in the next column. The supplied Hebrew ends with a comma and is preserved as supplied. The consulted Shabbat 54b names Rav Acha bar Ulla, Berakhot 12a has Rabbah bar Ulla, and Yevamot 77a has Rava bar Ulla. The passages attest those names. Hyman’s identification of these figures within his account remains a proposal.
